We spent the last 18 months building a feature-flag platform because we think shipping software shouldn't be scary, and flags shouldn't be an afterthought you bolt on at the end. They should be how a team delivers.

There are six of us. The money goes toward growing the engineering team and shipping faster for the customers who believed in us early. Thank you for that. Same to the team, and to Basis for betting on us.

L02:
Nine months, three teams, and more whiteboard sessions than I can count: this week we finished our migration from a monolith to microservices at the fintech where I work.

The number I care most about is p99 latency, which is down 40%. Deployments that used to take hours now take minutes, and the three teams ship independently without stepping on each other.

What surprised me is that the technical work was the easy part. The hard part was alignment. Getting three teams to agree on service boundaries, ownership, and standards took more energy than any line of code.

If I did it again I'd repeat the same three moves: start from the domain rather than the technology, migrate incrementally because big bangs fail, and celebrate the small wins, since nine months is a long time to go without one.

People say microservices are overhyped, and sometimes they are. This time they were the right tool. If you've survived a migration like this, I'd like to hear how yours went.
L03:
We're hiring a founding designer at our AI startup in Austin.

First design hire, reporting straight to the CEO. You'd define the visual identity and the design culture from scratch, and you'd own a real piece of the company: 0.5 to 1% equity.

I won't pretend the job is tidy. There's ambiguity everywhere, and the person who thrives here will sweat details nobody asked about. We want someone who treats design as a competitive advantage, because how humans interact with AI is one of the harder design problems going right now, and whoever takes this role gets to shape our answer to it.

Austin preferred, but we'll flex for the right person.

If this sounds like you, or like someone you know, comment or send me a DM. Referrals genuinely appreciated.
L04:
In January I was laid off from a big tech company. Six months later, I'm leading product at a 30-person startup.

The middle part was the hardest stretch of my career. I sent over 200 applications. Most disappeared into silence, some turned into interviews that went nowhere, and there were whole days where I questioned what I actually knew about my own value.

A few things held up. My job was not my identity, even when it felt like it was. And the right role was worth waiting for, which is easy to type now and was very hard to believe at the time.

If you're in the middle of a layoff search: the process is brutal and the silence is the worst part. It does end.

To the hiring managers who wrote actual, thoughtful rejections instead of form letters: thank you. Those mattered more than you probably realize.

My DMs are open if you're searching and want to talk.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same 3 foundation models.

Every week another one launches, and the pattern repeats: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing the actual work underneath. The prompt is not a moat. Anyone can copy a prompt in an afternoon.

What does create defensibility, as far as I can tell, is workflow depth and data. Get deep enough into how a team works that ripping you out hurts, and build feedback loops where usage makes the product better in ways a competitor can't shortcut.

The winners here won't be whoever has the best demo. They'll be whoever understands their customers' workflows better than anyone else.

If you're building in this space, one test: if the model providers shipped your feature tomorrow, what would be left?
L06:
Back from SaaStr Annual, where I met 40+ founders and sat through more sessions and hallway conversations than I can accurately count. Three things kept coming up.

PLG is maturing. Product-led growth has stopped being a slogan; the companies doing it well are getting genuinely sophisticated about layering sales on top of self-serve.

AI pricing is unsettled. Seats, usage, outcomes: every founder I asked is experimenting, and not one of them sounded confident. Nobody has cracked it.

Community-led growth is back. After a few quiet years, community is a live topic again, except this time with real ROI expectations attached.

The energy in SaaS right now is the highest I've felt in years. If you were there, I'm curious what stood out to you.
L07:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never make it to production. The instinct is to blame the models, but the models are ready. They have been for a while.

Two things actually kill pilots.

Data readiness. Most enterprises sit on fragmented, inconsistent, poorly governed data, and no model performs well on top of spreadsheets and silos.

Process redesign, or the lack of it. Companies bolt AI onto an existing workflow and expect magic. AI changes what the process should be, and if nobody rethinks it, the pilot dies right after the demo.

The companies getting AI into production aren't the ones with the best models. They did the unglamorous work first: cleaned their data, redesigned their processes, prepared their people for the change.

The models stopped being the bottleneck a while ago. The organizations around them haven't caught up.

L09:
Ten years in B2B sales, and the skill that has mattered most isn't pitching, negotiating, or objection handling. It's listening.

The call that taught me: a deal was falling apart, the prospect was airing concerns, and every instinct said jump in with answers. Instead I went quiet and stayed quiet, for 90 full seconds, on a live call. It felt like an hour.

Somewhere in that silence the prospect talked themselves through their own objection and surfaced the real blocker, one I never would have guessed. We closed two weeks later.

Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them if you give them the room. Sometimes the best discovery question is no question at all.

A decade in, and I still have to remind myself to shut up.
L10:
After 3 years, I'm shutting down Cartful. It's the hardest decision of my professional life.

We raised $1.1M, grew to 4,000 users, and never found repeatable revenue. That's the short version. The people who believed in us deserve the longer one, so here are the three lessons I'm taking with me.

Users are not customers. We celebrated signups while dodging the harder question of who would actually pay, and why.

Repeatable revenue beats everything. One-off deals feel like traction and are not. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one yet.

Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched ours to stay alive when we should have spent it finding out the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you, and I'm sorry we couldn't get there. The lessons were expensive. I intend to get my money's worth.
L11:
A few months ago I stopped running daily standups for my team of 14. We replaced them with async written updates: every morning each person posts what they did, what they're doing, and what's blocking them.

We got 6 hours of meetings back per week. Shipping speed didn't change at all. And engineers tell me they're getting longer uninterrupted stretches of real work.

The uncomfortable part was realizing our standup had mostly been for me. A status ritual dressed up as collaboration. Written updates do the same job better: people think before they write, everything is searchable later, and time zones stop mattering.

I'm not arguing standups are always wrong. But if yours feels like a status meeting, it probably is one, and your team figured that out before you did.
L12:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam.

Eleven weeks of studying around a full-time job, five practice exams, and more early mornings than I'd like to count. It's one of the hardest certifications I've attempted, and one of the more rewarding.

What actually worked, in case you're preparing: an hour a day beat cramming on Saturdays. The practice exams were the highest-value thing I did; each of the five exposed gaps I didn't know I had. Hands-on labs made concepts stick where videos didn't. And I put study time on my calendar like a meeting, because otherwise it was the first thing to get dropped.

If you're grinding through a certification while working full time, it's a slog, but it's doable.

Now to actually put it to work.
L13:
A year ago I became an engineering manager. It's been the most humbling year of my career.

The hard part wasn't the meetings or the 1:1s or even the difficult conversations. It was learning to measure my output by the team's work instead of my own commits. For years my sense of a good day came from shipping: green squares, merged PRs, something I could point at. Then my output became invisible. A good week now means my 7 direct reports are unblocked, growing, and shipping while my own name shows up nowhere.

It took months to stop feeling like an impostor about that.

What I've actually learned: the team's success is the job, full stop. Most problems turn out to be communication problems in disguise. Clarity is the most useful thing I can hand anyone. And the urge to jump in and fix things myself is almost always the wrong urge.

If you're a new EM struggling with the identity shift, you're in good company. Apparently it's just part of the deal.
L14:
Our team of 9 SREs finally committed to writing runbooks, and on-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter.

The systems didn't get better. The knowledge just stopped living exclusively in people's heads.

What we actually did: every incident got a runbook entry, without exception. Every repeated page triggered a documentation review. We deleted stale docs as aggressively as we wrote new ones, and runbook quality went into our definition of done.

Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks, which is roughly why nobody writes them. But the return is real once you measure it: fewer 2 AM wake-ups, faster onboarding, less bus factor, calmer rotations.

If your team is drowning in pages, the fix is probably not another tool. It's writing things down.
L15:
After 3 years fully remote, our company went hybrid: 2 days a week in the office. Here's how it has actually gone.

Retention improved, and our numbers are better than they've been in two years. Onboarding is noticeably faster. Cross-team collaboration feels easier.

It also cost us. Two senior people quit over the change, and those losses genuinely hurt. Trust took a hit during the transition. And some days the office is half empty, which leaves people wondering why they commuted.

I've stopped believing there's a right answer to remote versus hybrid. Every model has tradeoffs and every policy disappoints someone. What we could control was honesty: we told the team exactly why we were making the change, and we accepted that some people would make a different call for their lives. I respect the ones who did.

Anyone telling you this problem is solved is selling something.
L16:
AI won't replace junior developers, but it is changing what "junior" means.

We hired 2 junior engineers on my team recently. Both use AI pair-programming tools daily, and they ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago. It isn't close.

The skills that make them valuable have shifted, though. Less memorizing syntax and grinding out boilerplate. More reviewing code critically, asking the right questions, and understanding the system their code lands in. Today's junior orchestrates the tools, verifies the output, and starts learning architecture on day one.

Three consequences I'd bet on: hiring rubrics built around syntax trivia are obsolete. Mentorship matters more now, not less, because judgment can't be autocompleted. And the ladder from junior to senior is compressing.

Companies that stop hiring juniors because of AI aren't really saving money. They're quietly dismantling their future senior pipeline.
L17:
A churned customer came back last week, which made my month.

When they originally left, they told us plainly: our seat-based pricing punished them for growing their team. They were paying for licenses nobody used.

So we moved from seat-based to usage-based pricing. It was a scary switch. We modeled the downside a dozen times, and a few advisors told us flatly not to do it.

Since the change, expansion revenue is up 22%, sales conversations start with value instead of license counts, and churned customers have started coming back on their own.

The thing I underestimated: pricing tells customers whose side you're on. Seat-based pricing paid us when customers overbought. Usage-based pricing pays us only when they succeed. That alignment turned out to be worth more than the spreadsheet said.
L18:
Six months ago a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them. This week they signed an offer as a frontend developer at an insurance company.

The hard work was entirely theirs. For the record, here's what we did together: weekly check-ins even when progress felt slow, code reviews on real projects instead of toy exercises, 4 mock interviews with each round harder than the last, and some honest conversations about rejection and resilience.

What I didn't expect to learn: mentorship is mostly consistency. Not having all the answers, just showing up when someone's confidence is wobbling.

People love to debate whether bootcamp grads can make it in this industry. This one did, with grit and a bit of support, and I doubt they're unusual.

If you've got experience to spare, an hour a week is enough to move someone's career. And to my mentee, if you're reading: congratulations. You earned every bit of it.
L19:
We changed one email subject line and open rates jumped 31%.

For months our emails to 18k subscribers led with the feature: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Respectable open rates, nothing special. Then we tried describing the outcome instead, what the reader would actually get out of it. Same email, same list, same send time, one change.

Feature version: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard."
Outcome version: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking."

One talks about us. The other talks about them. It's the oldest lesson in marketing and we still needed the reminder: people don't care about your features, they care about what the features do for them.

We've since rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails the same way, and the gains have held.

If you write email for a living, pull up your last 10 subject lines and count how many are about you rather than the reader.
L20:
People ask how a 12-person team stays productive without a real ops function. We run the whole company on 5 tools.

Linear holds every task, bug, and project. If it isn't in Linear, it doesn't exist. Notion is the company brain: docs, wikis, meeting notes, onboarding. Slack handles communication, with strict channel hygiene to keep the noise down. Figma is where product ideas take shape before anyone writes code. And Otto, our homegrown deploy bot, moves code from PR to production on a single command. Everyone's favorite teammate.

That's the entire stack. Nothing overlaps, and nobody has to ask which doc is the source of truth.

The reasoning: every new tool charges a tax in context switching, licenses, onboarding, and integrations. We only add one when the pain of not having it beats the tax. So far, keeping it simple has been an advantage in itself.

Which tool could your team not give up? The answer usually says a lot about how the team really works.
L21:
I just took my first real break in 4 years: two weeks, no Slack, no email, no "quick calls."

The first few days were genuinely uncomfortable. I kept checking my phone out of habit, felt guilty, and half convinced myself things would fall apart without me. They did not.

The useful part came after I got back. Looking at my calendar with fresh eyes, it was obvious how much of my busyness was self-inflicted. In my first week back I killed 3 recurring meetings, and nobody has missed them. I also noticed how tired I had been, which at some point I'd apparently decided was normal.

Two things I now believe about rest: the work is never finished, so waiting until it is means never resting. And if a business can't survive two weeks without you, that's a design flaw in the business, not proof of your importance.

If you've been grinding for years without a real break, the sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need.
L22:
Three years ago we were 4 people in a garage in Denver. This week we hired employee #50.

I keep going back through old photos of that garage: the folding tables, the space heater, the whiteboard we bought off Craigslist. We serve 900 customers now, but the numbers only tell part of it.

What I'm proudest of is that the values we scribbled on that Craigslist whiteboard still guide how we operate: customers first, default to transparency, hire people better than yourself.

To the first 4, thank you for believing when there was very little to believe in. To the 46 who came after, thank you for choosing us. And to our 900 customers: everything we do is for you.

A milestone like this deserves a pause and a thank you. That done, back to work.
L23:
Networking events are mostly useless. I say that as someone who used to attend everything: conferences, mixers, founder happy hours. I collected hundreds of business cards. Number of clients that came out of all of it: zero.

My last 3 clients came from the same place, and it wasn't a conference. They found me through my writing online.

Writing wins on scale, because a post reaches thousands where a conversation reaches one. It wins on selection, because the right people arrive already sold on how you think. And it compounds: a good post keeps working for months, while a handshake is forgotten by Monday.

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

To be clear, relationships still matter enormously. But the best ones I have started when someone read something I wrote and thought, "this person gets it."

Publish your thinking. Your next client probably isn't at a conference. They're somewhere in a feed, and they can only find you if you've written something worth finding.
L24:
I joined Supply Chain Weekly for episode 142 to talk about AI demand forecasting.

We got into why traditional forecasting breaks down in volatile markets, what AI-driven forecasting actually looks like in practice once you get past the buzzwords, and the number I keep coming back to: at one of our pilot customers, forecast error is down 18%. That translates directly into less overstock, fewer stockouts, and working capital freed up.

Credit to the hosts for letting the conversation get into the unglamorous parts too: data quality, change management, and why the forecasting team's expertise matters more with AI in the loop, not less.

If you work in supply chain, operations, or planning, give episode 142 a listen. Link in the comments.
L25:
Our year in review: ARR went from $1.2M to $3.4M, the team grew from 9 to 21, and NPS sits at 61.

By most measures it was the best year in the company's history, and the NPS is the number I'm proudest of, because growth means very little if customers don't actually love what you build.

Now the mistake. We hired sales too early. We brought on reps before we, the founders, had figured out the sales motion ourselves, and the result was months of missed targets, frustrated reps, and expensive lessons. None of that was their fault. You can't hand someone a playbook you haven't written.

We eventually rebuilt the process from first principles and it clicked, but I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing this because year-in-review posts tend to be highlight reels, and growth is messier than that. If you're a founder about to make your first sales hires, sell it yourself first.
